The [posterior-distribution page](posterior-distributions.qmd#updating-a-continuous-parameter) normalized a continuous update by recognizing a beta density. A prior is **conjugate** to a likelihood when the resulting posterior belongs to the same distribution family as the prior.

Recall that a [likelihood](maximum-likelihood.qmd#probability-and-likelihood) holds the observed indicators fixed while varying the candidate parameter. Conditional [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) lets the Bernoulli contributions multiply, after which the prior and likelihood powers can be collected.

The calculation has one basic move: multiply the Bernoulli likelihood by the beta prior and collect like powers of $\theta$ and $1-\theta$. Those powers will identify the posterior family. We can then recover the normalizing constant and ask what the calculation has established. It simplifies the update, but it supplies no evidence that the sampling model fits the data.

## The exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model likelihood and prior

The exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model treats the Turkish UniMorph indicators as draws from a counterfactual exchangeable superpopulation:

$$
Z_i\mid\Theta=\theta
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta).
$$

The 120 sampled UniMorph rows contain 42 *t*-initial endings. Each row records a lexical type in one paradigm cell and carries no corpus token count. The rows were drawn without replacement from the 588-row UniMorph table.

```{r}
#| label: load-unimorph-conjugacy
library(ggplot2)

sample_120 <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-sample-120.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
n <- nrow(sample_120)
k <- sum(sample_120$t_initial)

unit_count <- 1L
alpha <- unit_count
beta <- unit_count
alpha_post <- alpha + k
beta_post <- beta + n - k

stopifnot(n == 120L, k == 42L)
data.frame(n, k, non_t_initial = n - k, alpha_post, beta_post)
```

For a $\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$ prior,

$$
f_\Theta(\theta)
=
\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1},
\qquad 0<\theta<1.
$$

Conditional independence gives the likelihood

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)
&=
\prod_{i=1}^n
\theta^{z_i}(1-\theta)^{1-z_i}\\
&=
\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}.
\end{aligned}
$$

## Collecting powers

Bayes' rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)
&\propto
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)f_\Theta(\theta)\\
&\propto
\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}
\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}\\
&=
\theta^{\alpha+k-1}
(1-\theta)^{\beta+n-k-1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The proportionality sign suppresses factors that do not vary with $\theta$: the prior constant $1/B(\alpha,\beta)$ and the evidence $p_{\mathbf Z}(\mathbf z)$. We can drop them while identifying the posterior [**kernel**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html), meaning the part of a density that contains its parameter-dependent shape. We must restore a normalizing constant before treating that shape as a probability density.

Only $k=\sum_i z_i$ and $n-k$ remain after the powers are collected. Thus the order of the binary observations disappears from this exchangeable likelihood. This is a consequence of the model's factorization, not permission to ignore source order when order carries dependence.

This is the kernel of another beta density:

$$
\Theta\mid\mathbf z
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+k,\beta+n-k).
$$

Thus the two posterior shape parameters are obtained by adding the focal and nonfocal counts to the corresponding prior shapes. With the support-calibrated $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$ prior, the result is a beta distribution with shape parameters `r alpha_post` and `r beta_post`.

The uniform prior is compatible with the $0<\theta<1$ support and makes the algebra visible. It is not uniquely neutral: a distribution uniform in $\theta$ is not uniform in the log odds, and alternative beta shapes would encode different prior predictive commitments.

```{r}
#| label: plot-unimorph-conjugacy
#| fig-cap: "Beta prior and posterior for the exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model, calculated from the observed 42 of 120 lexeme cells."
theta <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1001L)
density <- rbind(
  data.frame(theta, value = dbeta(theta, alpha, beta),
             distribution = "Beta(1, 1) prior"),
  data.frame(theta, value = dbeta(theta, alpha_post, beta_post),
             distribution = sprintf("Beta(%d, %d) posterior",
                                    alpha_post, beta_post))
)

ggplot(density, aes(theta, value, linetype = distribution)) +
  geom_line(color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.85) +
  labs(x = "Modeled share of t-initial lexeme cells", y = "Density",
       linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## The normalizing constant

Recognizing the kernel supplies the constant that makes the density integrate to one:

$$
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)
=
\frac{1}{B(\alpha+k,\beta+n-k)}
\theta^{\alpha+k-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta+n-k-1}.
$$

The beta function is

$$
B(a,b)
=
\int_0^1t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Conjugacy makes this calculation algebraic. It does not establish that the exchangeable Bernoulli likelihood matches the data-collection design.

## What conjugacy buys, and what it does not

The update is computationally convenient: it provides a normalized posterior, closed-form moments, and beta-binomial predictive masses. But convenience is separate from measurement and sampling. The known UniMorph resource contains 200 focal cells among 588, so the actual finite-population design is hypergeometric. The exchangeable Bernoulli model is a working superpopulation model rather than an analysis of uncertainty about the file.

## Recap and forward link

1. A kernel preserves density shape while omitting constants independent of $\theta$.
2. Multiplying beta and Bernoulli powers adds observed counts to prior shapes.
3. The beta-function constant turns the recognized kernel into a normalized density.
4. Conjugacy supplies algebraic convenience, not evidence for the sampling assumptions.

The [prior-predictive page](prior-predictive-distributions.qmd#from-a-parameter-prior-to-possible-counts) asks what the chosen prior and likelihood predict before observing the sample.

## Check your understanding

1. Which exponents are added in the beta--Bernoulli update?
2. Why can order be omitted from this likelihood?
3. What does recognizing the beta kernel provide?
4. Why does conjugacy not justify the independent-draw assumption?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The prior exponents $\alpha-1$ and $\beta-1$ receive the focal count $k$ and nonfocal count $n-k$, yielding shapes $\alpha+k$ and $\beta+n-k$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Conditional exchangeability makes every ordered binary sequence with the same $k$ contribute the same likelihood kernel $\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Recognizing the beta kernel provides the normalized beta posterior, including its beta-function constant, moments, and predictive distribution. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Conjugacy is an algebraic relation between a prior and likelihood; it supplies no evidence that independent draws match the actual without-replacement design. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
